exercises.title: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - ADR status lifecycle, context sections, decision rationale, honest consequences, and managing historical ADRs. Capture the "why" behind technical decisions.

questions.q: A team starts writing ADRs. An ADR's Status field currently says "Proposed." What does this mean for the team?
options: The decision was made in the past but has since been reversed
The decision has been made and is now final
The ADR has been written and shared for review but the decision has not yet been formally accepted - it is open for discussion and may be amended or rejected
The ADR is a draft and hasn't been shared with anyone yet
questions.explanation: ADR status values track the lifecycle of a decision. The most commonly used statuses are: Proposed - written, shared, open for review and discussion Accepted - the team has agreed to this decision and will implement it Deprecated - this decision was once accepted but is no longer in effect Superseded by ADR-NNN - this decision was replaced by a newer one (link provided) Rejected - the proposal was discussed and not adopted Why status matters: ADRs accumulate over time. Without clear status, a future engineer reading ADR-007 can't tell if it reflects current practice or a 3-year-old decision that was replaced. "Superseded by ADR-023" creates a navigable chain of reasoning. ADR status vocabulary examples: "Status: Proposed" → "Status: Accepted (2026-04-07, agreed by backend team)" "Status: Superseded by ADR-023 (2026-03-15) - we moved from PostgreSQL to CockroachDB for global distribution" "Status: Deprecated - this pattern was abandoned when we moved to microservices"

questions.q: An ADR's "Context" section reads: "We need to choose a database." A principal engineer rejects this as insufficient. What does a strong context section contain?
options: A list of all databases that were evaluated
The team members who were involved in the decision
The decision that was made
The specific forces, constraints, requirements, and current state that make this decision necessary - enough context for someone joining the company in 3 years to understand why a decision was needed
questions.explanation: The ADR Context section answers: "Why was this decision even necessary? What situation forced us here?" Weak context: "We need to choose a database." Strong context: "Our current single-node PostgreSQL instance serves 3 read-heavy microservices. As of Q1 2026, peak read load exceeds the connection limit (500 connections). The services compete for connections, causing intermittent 503 errors. We need a solution that: • Handles at least 2,000 concurrent read connections • Requires no changes to the existing SQL query patterns • Can be deployed within the current infrastructure (AWS RDS or self-managed on EKS) • Fits within the team's existing Postgres expertise" What context should establish: • The current state (what exists today) • The problem or constraint (why the current state is insufficient) • Specific requirements or constraints (non-negotiables) • Team context (skills, existing tools, budget) • Timing or urgency ADR context vocabulary: "At the time of this decision, …" "The current approach has the following limitations: …" "The following constraints drive this decision: …" "We require a solution that: …"

questions.q: An ADR's "Decision" section reads: "We will use PostgreSQL with read replicas." A tech lead says the decision statement is correct but incomplete. What is the most important thing to add?
options: The names of engineers who agreed to the decision
The expected timeline for implementation
The rationale - a brief explanation of WHY this decision was made over alternatives
A link to the PostgreSQL documentation
questions.explanation: The Decision section must state both what was decided AND why - otherwise the ADR is just a record of what was done, not a record of the reasoning. Weak decision statement: "We will use PostgreSQL with read replicas." Strong decision statement: "We will add 2 read replicas to our existing PostgreSQL instance. This approach was chosen because: • It requires no changes to existing SQL queries (unlike moving to a different database engine) • It is within the team's current operational expertise • It addresses the connection limit issue without a disruptive migration • Estimated cost increase: ~$340/month, within approved infrastructure budget The alternative (migrating to PgBouncer connection pooler) was rejected for now due to query compatibility unknowns (see ADR-Alternatives)." Why the "why" matters: In 2 years, a new engineer will read this ADR and ask "but why not use connection pooling?" Without the reasoning, they will either repeat the analysis wastefully or make a change that undoes the original decision without understanding its context. Decision vocabulary: "We will adopt X because: …" "We chose X over Y based on: …" "This decision is driven by: …" "We accept the trade-off of [X] in exchange for [Y]."

questions.q: An ADR includes a "Consequences" section. An engineer asks: "This section says the decision creates both positive and negative consequences. Should we hide the negative ones?" What is the correct answer?
options: The Consequences section is optional; experienced teams skip it
No - the Consequences section must honestly list both positive and negative outcomes; hiding negatives defeats the purpose of the ADR and misleads future decision-makers
Yes - negative consequences make the decision look weak and may cause stakeholders to reject it
Only list negative consequences - positive ones are obvious
questions.explanation: The Consequences section is what separates a genuine ADR from a post-hoc justification document. What Consequences should list: Positive consequences: "This eliminates connection limit errors immediately." "The team can implement this within 1 sprint using existing skills." Negative consequences / trade-offs accepted: "Read replicas add replication lag - reads from replicas may return data up to 100ms old." "The team must now manage replica health monitoring and failover testing." "This is a temporary solution - at 10x current load, we will need to revisit sharding or a different database." Why honesty is essential: • Future engineers who encounter the replication lag problem can look back and see: "yes, the team knew about this and accepted it" • It prevents the "but who decided this?" blame game • It enables smarter future decisions: "ADR-012 said this would need revisiting at 10x load - we're there now" Consequences vocabulary: "The positive effect is: …" "The accepted trade-off is: …" "This introduces risk of: …" "Future teams should be aware that: …" "This decision will need to be revisited when: …"

questions.q: A team has 47 ADRs. An engineer proposes deleting ADR-003 because "we don't use that technology anymore." The tech lead says this is wrong. What should be done instead?
options: Delete ADR-003 and update the ADR index
Archive ADR-003 in a separate folder
Update ADR-003's status to "Superseded by ADR-031" and add a note explaining that the technology was replaced and when - preserving the historical record
Keep ADR-003 as-is and rely on engineers to check all ADRs before making decisions
questions.explanation: ADRs are a historical record of decision-making, not a current state documentation system. Deleting or hiding decisions destroys the organisational memory that ADRs are designed to preserve. Why "Superseded by ADR-031" is the right approach: • It preserves the original reasoning - future engineers can see what was decided AND what replaced it • It creates a chain of decisions - ADR-003 links to ADR-031 which may link to ADR-047 • It shows the evolution of thinking: "we tried approach A, it had problem X, so we moved to approach B" • It prevents re-litigating old decisions - "we already considered this in 2023" The ADR amendment pattern: 1. Write a new ADR explaining what changed and why 2. Mark the old ADR as "Superseded by ADR-[new number]" 3. Add "Supersedes ADR-[old number]" to the new ADR 4. Add a brief note to the old ADR: "This approach was replaced in 2026 when [reason]." What to preserve in a supersession note: "Status: Superseded by ADR-031 (2026-04-07). We replaced this approach because the chosen library was abandoned and we moved to [alternative]. See ADR-031 for the current decision."

questions.q: Reviewer: 'Hey team, I'm looking at this PR and noticed a missing ADR for the new user authentication flow. It seems like we're just blindly implementing the API endpoint without documenting *why* we chose this approach. Project Manager: 'Yeah, that's what I was hoping to discuss with you - are we capturing these architectural decisions properly?'
options: The Project Manager is asking if the reviewer understands the technical implications of the authentication flow.

The Project Manager is concerned about whether the team is consistently documenting architectural decisions, specifically regarding the rationale behind choices like this API endpoint, to ensure maintainability and future understanding.
The Project Manager believes the reviewer should focus solely on ensuring the code adheres to existing coding standards.
The Project Manager wants the reviewer to simply add a comment explaining the API endpoint implementation in the PR description.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights a critical aspect of ADRs: they aren't just about stating decisions but documenting the *reasoning* behind them. The Project Manager is raising a concern that the team isn't consistently providing context for architectural choices, which can lead to problems when the code needs to be maintained or modified later. Option A misinterprets the question as purely technical; option D focuses on just adding a comment without addressing the broader need for documentation. Option C is entirely irrelevant.

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I'm reviewing this PR for the new payment processing service. The developer just implemented the webhook endpoint against the existing MySQL database - no ADR! It seems like we're taking a significant risk by not documenting why we chose MySQL over PostgreSQL or even a NoSQL solution. This feels like a potential disaster waiting to happen." Mark : "Relax, Sarah. We've been using MySQL for years; it works perfectly fine." Which of the following is the MOST appropriate response from the team lead regarding Mark's comment?
options: insufficient - the PR doesn't technically violate any coding standards.
correct - Mark is right, and Sarah should focus on code quality instead.
incorrect - the team lead should acknowledge Sarah's concerns and initiate a discussion about documenting architectural decisions.
incorrect - the team lead should immediately shut down the PR until an ADR is created.
questions.explanation: The correct answer highlights the core purpose of ADRs: to provide justification for technical choices. While Mark's experience with MySQL might be valid, it doesn't negate the need for documented reasoning when introducing new services or making significant changes. The team lead needs to address the *lack* of documentation and guide the developer toward creating an ADR to mitigate potential risks. Options A and B are inaccurate - a lack of ADRs isn't simply about coding standards; it's about architectural risk management. Option C is also incorrect as addressing Sarah's concerns is paramount.

options: Ask Mark if he considered using Stripe's SDK for easier integration.
Recommend that Mark ignore the ADR requirement and proceed.
Tell Mark to prioritize fixing the code first, then document.
Suggest the team add a 'Consequences' section outlining potential problems.
questions.explanation: Mark is correctly pointing out a deficiency in the ADR process. questions.q: PR Description: 'Implemented the new user profile API endpoint using REST principles and JSON format. This improves data accessibility for mobile clients. No ADR required.'
options: This description is perfectly adequate; it fulfills all ADR requirements.
It's too verbose and should be shortened to focus on the technical details.
The description needs a section detailing the expected API response times.
It's insufficient-the description lacks justification for *why* REST was chosen over GraphQL.
questions.explanation: The PR description is inadequate because it doesn't explain *why* REST was chosen over alternative approaches like GraphQL. A key purpose of an ADR is to document the reasoning behind technical decisions, particularly when trade-offs are involved. Simply stating that REST improves data accessibility isn't sufficient justification.

exercises.title: Architecture Decision Record (ADR) Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practice ADR vocabulary: capturing context, status lifecycle, significant decisions, superseding ADRs, and the MADR format.

questions.q: An ADR template says 'The ADR captures the context for future engineers.' What does the context section explain?
options: The current bug count
The situation and forces at play when the decision was made - the problem being solved, the constraints, alternatives considered, and why the chosen option was selected at that time
The names of engineers who disagreed
The technical implementation details
questions.explanation: The context section is the most valuable part of an ADR for future engineers. Systems are built by people with shared knowledge that is never written down. The context section captures: what problem this solves, what constraints existed, what was considered, and why the chosen approach was selected - preventing 'why did we do this?!' confusion years later.

questions.q: An ADR has 'Status: Proposed.' What does the ADR lifecycle typically look like?
options: Only two states: Active and Inactive
Proposed (under discussion) → Accepted (approved and guiding development) → Deprecated (superseded or context no longer applies). Some teams also use Rejected for considered-but-rejected decisions
Status is only updated annually
Status is set automatically by the CI system
questions.explanation: ADR status tracks where a decision is in its lifecycle: Proposed means it's been drafted and is under review; Accepted means it's been agreed upon and should guide development; Deprecated or Superseded means a newer ADR has replaced it. This allows teams to know which decisions are still in force.

questions.q: Your team says 'We write an ADR when a significant decision is made.' What qualifies as a significant decision?
options: Every code review comment
Any decision that affects the architecture, is hard to reverse, has cross-team impact, or that future team members would benefit from understanding the rationale for
Only decisions made by the CTO
Only decisions about cloud providers
questions.explanation: Significant decisions worthy of an ADR include: choosing a database, selecting an architectural pattern, deciding how to handle authentication, choosing a communication protocol, or deciding to adopt a new framework. The test: 'Will a future engineer wonder why we did this?' If yes, write an ADR.

questions.q: An ADR header says 'This ADR is superseded by ADR-042.' What does superseding mean in ADR practice?
options: ADR-042 deleted the current ADR
A newer decision (ADR-042) replaces the current one - the old ADR is kept for history but marked as no longer the current guidance, with a link to the new one
The current ADR overrides ADR-042
Superseded means the decision was rejected
questions.explanation: ADRs are never deleted - they are historical records. When a decision changes, a new ADR is written and the old one is marked 'Superseded by ADR-042.' This preserves the history of why the original decision was made, what changed, and when - valuable context for understanding how the system evolved.

questions.q: A team says 'We use MADR (Markdown ADR) format.' What is MADR?
options: A proprietary enterprise ADR tool
A lightweight, standardized Markdown template for ADRs that includes sections for title, status, context, decision, and consequences - designed to be stored in version control alongside code
A database for storing architecture decisions
A tool that automatically generates ADRs from code comments
questions.explanation: MADR (Markdown Architectural Decision Records) is a community-maintained template standard for ADRs written in Markdown - making them easy to store in a Git repository alongside the code they document. The standardized format makes ADRs consistent and easy to scan across a large codebase.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'I'm seeing a lot of boilerplate in this PR. Could you justify the decision to use this specific logging library instead of our standard one? It seems like we're adding unnecessary complexity here."
options: insufficient - the account balance is too low...
redundant - the code duplicates functionality already present.
justification - a clear explanation of the rationale behind technical choices is crucial for maintainability and understanding.
ambiguous - the reviewer's comment lacks specific terminology related to architectural decisions.
questions.explanation: The question centers around the core purpose of an ADR. The reviewer's comment highlights a situation where a developer needs to provide a 'justification' for their technical choices. An ADR provides that justification-it's not simply stating what was done but *why* it was done, detailing the reasoning and potential trade-offs involved in architectural decisions like library selection. Option A is incorrect because an account balance isn't relevant; option C misinterprets the reviewer's comment as a request for justification, while option D describes a vague communication style that doesn't align with ADR principles.

questions.q: PR Description: Subject: Implement User Authentication API We're implementing a new user authentication API endpoint. This ADR outlines the decision to use JWT (JSON Web Tokens) for session management instead of our legacy cookie-based system. We believe JWT offers improved security and scalability. Reviewer Comment: 'I appreciate the clarity, but can you elaborate on why we've chosen JWT over cookies? The team is concerned about potential key rotation challenges with JWT in a high-traffic environment.'
options: Insufficient - the PR doesn't explain the security benefits of JWT.
Correct - the PR clearly states the decision and acknowledges reviewer concerns about key rotation, demonstrating proactive communication.
Incorrect - the PR focuses solely on scalability advantages without addressing potential risks or justifications for the chosen technology.
The PR is overly verbose and requires significantly more detail regarding the authentication flow.
questions.explanation: This question assesses understanding of how ADRs should address concerns raised during code review. The correct answer highlights that a good ADR proactively anticipates potential issues like key rotation and explicitly justifies technical decisions. Options A and C misrepresent the role of an ADR - it's not just about stating the decision, but also explaining the rationale and addressing potential objections. Option D is too general; the PR *does* contain justification, though perhaps more could be added.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'I'm reviewing this ADR for the new payment processing flow. The description mentions we're opting for a microservice architecture to handle transactions. But I'm seeing no discussion around potential data consistency issues - specifically, eventual consistency versus strong consistency in a system handling financial operations. Shouldn't we have addressed that explicitly?'
options: insufficient - the ADR doesn't detail the chosen consistency model.
correct - the ADR should always include a full technical justification for architectural decisions.
adequate - the ADR mentions 'scalability,' which implicitly addresses potential consistency challenges in a distributed system.
redundant - the reviewer's concern is already covered by the broader discussion of 'high availability'.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of the *purpose* of an ADR. While scalability and high availability are related to architectural decisions, a strong ADR must explicitly address potential trade-offs like consistency models - especially in critical areas like payments. The reviewer is rightly pointing out that merely stating 'we're using microservices' doesn't cover the fundamental technical implications for data integrity. The correct answer emphasizes that ADRs need to be *comprehensive* and proactively identify and discuss potential risks.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'Okay, the ADR for this new API gateway is well-written. However, I'm noticing you've decided to use gRPC for inter-service communication instead of REST. Can you explain the rationale behind that choice? We haven't used gRPC before, and there are concerns about increased complexity and a steeper learning curve.'
options: Insufficient - the ADR simply states 'gRPC provides better performance'.
Correct - the ADR clearly outlines the performance benefits of gRPC in reducing latency for data transfer.

The ADR should include a discussion of potential operational overhead, like increased monitoring needs and specialized tooling requirements associated with gRPC, alongside the performance gains. It also needs to address the team's lack of experience.
The ADR is only relevant to the business stakeholders; developers shouldn't be involved in architectural decisions.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding beyond just the *technical* benefits of gRPC. A good ADR needs to justify architectural choices with a full consideration of the trade-offs - in this case, acknowledging the increased complexity and operational costs alongside performance improvements. Simply stating 'better performance' isn't sufficient justification for a significant change like adopting a new protocol; the team's lack of experience is also a critical factor to address.

questions.q: PR Description: Subject: Migrate to PostgreSQL Database The team has decided to migrate our core application database from MySQL to PostgreSQL. This ADR outlines the decision based on PostgreSQL's superior support for JSON data types and its robust features for handling large datasets. We anticipate this will improve query performance and reduce storage costs in the long run. Reviewer Comment: 'While I understand the benefits of PostgreSQL, I'm seeing no discussion about potential compatibility issues with our existing ORM (Object-Relational Mapper). Are we planning a full migration or a gradual switchover? Also, what's our rollback strategy if things go wrong?'
options: Insufficient - the database schema has not been fully documented.
Correct - the ADR adequately addresses the reviewer's concerns about migration strategy and risk mitigation.
Incorrect - the ADR fails to mention a plan for testing the new database with existing application code, potentially leading to unexpected issues during deployment.
Insufficient - the ADR doesn't provide any information about how the migration will impact current user experience.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of a key aspect of ADRs: proactively addressing potential risks. The correct answer acknowledges that the ADR discusses migration strategy and risk mitigation. Options A and B misrepresent the purpose of an ADR-it's not just about stating decisions but also outlining how those decisions will be implemented and managed, including contingency plans. Option C highlights a crucial missing element - testing - and option D focuses on a less critical concern (user experience) that should have been addressed within the broader migration plan.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a CONTRIBUTING.md file?
options: To list all contributors who have submitted pull requests
To explain how external contributors can submit issues, pull requests, and follow the project's development process
To document the project's license and copyright information
To describe the project's roadmap and upcoming features
questions.explanation: CONTRIBUTING.md guides potential contributors: how to set up a dev environment, the PR process, coding standards, how to report bugs, and what kinds of contributions are welcome.

questions.q: What does 'first-time contributor friendly' mean in an open-source project?
options: The project only accepts contributions from developers with no prior experience
The project labels simple issues as 'good first issue' and provides detailed setup documentation to lower the barrier for new contributors
The project requires contributors to sign a CLA before their first PR
The project prioritizes documentation contributions over code contributions
questions.explanation: First-time contributor friendliness is signaled by 'good first issue' labels, detailed onboarding docs, and a welcoming code of conduct. It lowers the barrier to entry for contributors unfamiliar with the codebase.

questions.q: What is a CLA (Contributor License Agreement)?
options: A checklist contributors must complete before submitting a PR
A legal agreement where contributors grant the project the right to use, modify, and distribute their contribution
A code quality standard that all contributions must meet
A community award given to top open-source contributors
questions.explanation: A CLA transfers or licenses the intellectual property rights of a contribution to the project. It ensures the project maintainers have the legal right to include and distribute the contributed code.

options: If something is broken, tell us.
Before opening a bug report, please search existing issues to avoid duplicates. Include your OS version, Node.js version, and a minimal reproducible example.
Bugs should be emailed to the maintainer directly.
All bugs must include a fix or they will be closed.
questions.explanation: Good bug reporting guidance reduces duplicate issues and provides maintainers with the information they need to reproduce and fix bugs. Minimal reproducible examples are especially valuable.

questions.q: What is the 'Code of Conduct' in an open-source project?
options: A document specifying the coding style and naming conventions
A community agreement that defines acceptable behavior and the consequences of unacceptable behavior to create a welcoming environment
A legal contract between the project and its corporate sponsors
A checklist for reviewing pull requests
questions.explanation: A Code of Conduct (commonly the Contributor Covenant) sets community behavior standards. It defines what constitutes harassment, how to report violations, and how maintainers will respond.

questions.q: What does 'DCO (Developer Certificate of Origin)' require contributors to do?
options: Sign a legal contract with the project's sponsoring organization
Add a 'Signed-off-by' line to each commit certifying they have the right to submit the code under the project's license
Pass a code review certification before their first contribution is accepted
Provide their real name and employer in their GitHub profile
questions.explanation: The DCO is a lightweight alternative to a CLA. Contributors add 'Signed-off-by: Name ' to commits, certifying they wrote the code or have the right to submit it under the project's open-source license.

We don't accept this kind of contribution.
Close without comment.

A security scanner that checks for outdated dependencies
A tool that notifies contributors when their PR has merge conflicts

exercises.title: Decision Brief Writing
exercises.subtitle: 4 exercises - write decision briefs that frame the problem, compare options fairly, and recommend a path with clear rationale and risks.

questions.q: You are writing a decision brief for leadership on whether to migrate from REST to GraphQL. Which opening correctly frames the "Problem" section?
options: "We should probably use GraphQL, it's more modern."
"Our mobile team currently makes 6-8 separate REST calls per screen load, causing over-fetching and slow load times on low-bandwidth connections. We need to decide on an approach to reduce this."
"Someone suggested GraphQL in a meeting."
"GraphQL vs REST: a comparison."
questions.explanation: A decision brief's Problem section should state the concrete, measurable pain point driving the need for a decision - not the proposed solution and not a vague preference. This gives readers the "why now" before they see any options. Formula: "[Team/system] currently [specific symptom with numbers]. We need to decide [decision framed as a question]." Decision briefs are written for time-constrained readers (executives, leads) who need to understand the stakes in the first two sentences, not after ten paragraphs of background.

questions.q: The "Options" section of your decision brief needs to present three approaches. Which format is correct?
options: List every possible option you can think of, no matter how unlikely.
"Just go with whatever the tech lead prefers."

"Option A: Keep REST, add response caching. Option C: Migrate to GraphQL incrementally, screen by screen. Option D: Adopt a BFF (Backend-for-Frontend) layer. Each option below includes cost, risk, and timeline."
"There are many options, it depends."
questions.explanation: A good Options section presents a small, curated set (typically 2-4) of genuinely viable approaches, each labelled clearly (Option A/C/D) and evaluated on the same dimensions (cost, risk, timeline) so readers can compare like-for-like. Formula: "Option [X]: [one-line description]. [Cost/risk/timeline for each]." Avoid padding the list with strawman options included only to make the recommended option look better - decision-makers can usually tell, and it undermines trust in the brief.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly introduces the "Recommendation" section of a decision brief?
options: "We recommend Option A (incremental GraphQL migration) because it addresses the over-fetching problem within one quarter, requires no new infrastructure, and lets us revert per-screen if issues arise - the lowest-risk path to the stated goal."
"Option A seems fine I guess."
"We can't decide, please choose for us."
"We recommend Option A because it's the best."
questions.explanation: The Recommendation must name the chosen option and give specific, evidence-based reasons tied directly back to the problem statement - not a vague "it's the best" judgement. A decision brief exists precisely to make and justify a recommendation, not to present a neutral menu. Formula: "We recommend [Option X] because [reason 1], [reason 2], and [reason 3] - [summary tying back to the original problem]."

questions.q: A decision brief needs a "Risks" section for the recommended option. Which entry is correctly written?
options: "Risk: the incremental migration could create temporary inconsistency between REST and GraphQL responses during the transition period. Mitigation: feature-flag each screen's migration and roll back individually if data mismatches are detected."
"There might be some risks, we'll see."
"Risk: everything could go wrong."
"No risks, this option is perfect."
questions.explanation: A properly written risk entry names a specific, plausible failure mode and pairs it with a concrete mitigation - not a vague warning and not false confidence that no risk exists. Every non-trivial recommendation carries risk; hiding it damages credibility, and stating it with a mitigation builds trust. Formula: "Risk: [specific failure mode]. Mitigation: [specific counter-measure]." Leadership reading a decision brief expects risks to be surfaced proactively, not discovered later.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'I'm seeing a lot of `if` statements here handling different user roles. Could you clarify the logic and maybe consider a more role-based approach to reduce duplication? You're writing a decision brief for your team lead, outlining why a refactoring of this module is necessary. Which phrasing in the 'Justification' section best reflects the reviewer's concerns and prepares the reader for a proposed solution?
options: insufficient - the code violates DRY principles...
sufficient - it explains the technical debt without context.
appropriate - it clearly states the problem and suggests a direction for resolution.
adequate - it simply describes the current state of the code.
questions.explanation: The key here is framing the issue within the decision brief's purpose. Option 3 correctly acknowledges the problem (technical debt) and subtly guides the reader toward a potential solution - role-based design. Options A and D are too vague; they don't convey the urgency or specific technical concerns raised by the reviewer. Option C simply restates the issue without suggesting action, failing to justify the need for change.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'This API endpoint returns a 400 error when the input data is missing the 'userId' field. It's causing intermittent failures in our mobile app.' You are drafting a decision brief for your team to investigate and potentially fix this issue. Which of the following phrases best opens the 'Problem' section, accurately reflecting the reviewer's reported problem?
options: This issue stems from a lack of input validation within the API implementation.
The current API behavior introduces significant instability for our mobile users.
Insufficient - the API endpoint is currently functioning as designed.
A recent deployment introduced an error that causes intermittent 400 responses.
questions.explanation: This option most accurately reflects the reviewer's direct report . The other options introduce assumptions about the *reason* for the error (validation, deployment) or misrepresent the impact (functioning as designed). Framing the problem around the specific observed behavior - the 400 error and its effect on the mobile app - immediately establishes the scope of the investigation and demonstrates you've understood the core issue. It also provides context needed to guide subsequent discussion about root cause.

questions.q: You're tasked with writing a decision brief for your team to evaluate whether to adopt a new logging library. A senior developer comments on Slack: 'Hey @team, we're drowning in logs! It's so hard to filter and analyze them effectively. Seriously considering switching to something more structured.' Which of the following phrases best begins the 'Problem' section of your brief, accurately capturing the urgency and frustration expressed by the senior dev?
options: 'We have identified several potential logging libraries that could improve our monitoring efforts.'
'The primary challenge is the lack of centralized logging capabilities, leading to significant operational overhead.'
'A thorough assessment of our existing log management system will be conducted before recommending any changes.'
'This brief outlines a proposed solution for optimizing our current logging infrastructure.'
questions.explanation: The correct option directly addresses the core issue raised in the Slack message: the *problem* is the overwhelming volume and difficulty in managing logs. Options D and A focus on solutions or potential choices, while Option B succinctly states the problem's impact (operational overhead), mirroring the senior developer's frustration. Option C is too vague and doesn't acknowledge the specific challenge presented - a common mistake when framing problems in documentation.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'This PR introduces a new feature that allows users to upload images directly to the server. However, there's no rate limiting in place, and I'm concerned about potential abuse leading to denial-of-service attacks.' You are writing a decision brief for your team lead regarding this change. Which phrase best frames the 'Risks' section introduction?
options: insufficient - the PR lacks detailed testing coverage...
significant - uncontrolled uploads pose a serious security risk...
minor - rate limiting can be easily added as an afterthought...
negligible - the feature is unlikely to attract malicious actors directly >
questions.explanation: The correct answer highlights the significant nature of the risk. The reviewer explicitly raised concerns about a potential denial-of-service attack due to a lack of rate limiting. Options A and B focus on testing or trivial issues, while option C minimizes the problem and D is overly dismissive - a good decision brief needs to acknowledge and prioritize serious risks like this one. Framing it as 'significant' immediately establishes the importance of addressing the vulnerability.

exercises.title: Writing Design Documents (English)
exercises.subtitle: 8 exercises - practise the vocabulary and structure of technical design documents: goals, non-goals, alternatives considered, and design decisions.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a 'Goals' section in a design document?
options: To list the team members responsible for the project
To clearly state what the proposed design aims to achieve - the success criteria
To describe the existing system that will be replaced
To list the technical requirements approved by the architecture team
questions.explanation: The Goals section defines what success looks like for this design. It allows reviewers to evaluate whether the proposed solution actually achieves the stated objectives.

questions.q: Why do design documents include a 'Non-Goals' section?
options: To list features that were rejected by management
To explicitly state what is out of scope, preventing scope creep and focusing the design review
To document bugs that will not be fixed in this iteration
To describe the system's limitations for security auditors
questions.explanation: Non-goals define boundaries. Stating 'this design does not address multi-region support' prevents reviewers from expecting it and keeps discussions focused on what the design actually solves.

questions.q: What should the 'Alternatives Considered' section of a design doc contain?
options: A list of all open-source libraries evaluated during the project
Other design options that were evaluated, with an explanation of why they were not chosen
The names of engineers who proposed different solutions
A comparison of pricing for different cloud providers
questions.explanation: Alternatives Considered documents the trade-off analysis. It shows that the team explored the solution space and explains why the chosen approach is better for this context.

questions.q: Which sentence is an example of good 'Design Decision' language in a design doc?
options: We chose PostgreSQL because it is the best database.
We chose PostgreSQL over DynamoDB for this use case because our query patterns require ad-hoc joins, and our data volume (
PostgreSQL was selected by the CTO.
We will use PostgreSQL and figure out the details later.
questions.explanation: Good design decision language states the choice, the alternatives, the specific reason for the choice, and the context (query patterns, data volume). Vague or authority-based justifications are not useful for future readers.

questions.q: What is 'open questions' section in a design document used for?
options: Listing questions from the last team meeting that went unanswered
Documenting unresolved decisions or areas of uncertainty that need input before the design is finalized
Collecting feedback from stakeholders after the design is implemented
Tracking bugs discovered during implementation
questions.explanation: Open questions flag areas where the author is unsure, needs input, or where the team must make a decision before implementation begins. They invite focused review from the right people.

questions.q: What distinguishes a design document from an RFC (Request for Comments)?

An RFC explicitly invites community or team feedback and discussion; a design doc may be more internal and implementation-focused

questions.q: What is the primary audience consideration when writing a developer onboarding guide?
options: The document is for the author to remember the setup steps
The reader is brand new to the codebase and team; they need clear step-by-step instructions and cannot rely on implied knowledge
The document is reviewed annually by security auditors
The reader is an experienced developer who only needs high-level pointers
questions.explanation: Onboarding docs are written for someone with zero context about the specific codebase and team. Every implied step or unexplained term is a potential blocker for a new joiner.

questions.q: Which element is most important to include in an environment setup guide?
options: The history of why the project was created
Exact commands to run, expected outputs, and how to verify success at each step
The team org chart and who to ask for what
Performance benchmarks for the development environment
questions.explanation: Setup guides must be executable. Every step needs the exact command, and ideally shows what successful output looks like so the reader knows whether the step worked.

options: The performance review schedule for new employees
What a new joiner is expected to learn, contribute, and own during their first 30, 60, and 90 days
The release schedule for the product during the new hire's first quarter
The frequency of 1:1 meetings between the new hire and their manager
questions.explanation: A 30-60-90 day plan sets expectations: 30 days = learning the codebase and process; 60 days = making small contributions; 90 days = owning a feature or area. It gives new joiners a clear ramp-up path.

options: Leave it out to avoid discouraging new joiners
Document the symptom, the workaround, and link to the issue tracker entry so the reader is not blocked and knows the team is aware
Ask the new joiner to figure it out as a learning exercise
Add a general note that 'setup may have issues on some machines'
questions.explanation: Known issues that new joiners hit repeatedly should be documented with symptoms, workarounds, and context. This saves hours of debugging time and shows the team is maintaining the docs.

questions.q: What is 'evergreen documentation' in the context of onboarding?
options: Documentation that is never updated because it covers stable topics
Documentation that is actively maintained so it remains accurate as the system evolves, rather than becoming stale
Documentation written in plain English without technical jargon
Documentation stored in a version control system
questions.explanation: Evergreen docs stay current. Teams often achieve this by linking docs to the code review process (docs updated when related code changes), assigning doc owners, or scheduling periodic reviews.

Our system consists of three main services: the API gateway (handles all client requests), the worker service (processes background jobs), and the data pipeline (ingests and transforms events). Each service communicates via a message queue.
See the Confluence page for architecture details.
The architecture was designed in 2019 and has evolved significantly since then.
questions.explanation: A good architecture overview names the components, explains what each does in one sentence, and describes how they relate. This gives a new joiner a mental model before diving into code.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a 'Glossary' section in onboarding docs?
options: To impress new joiners with the team's technical vocabulary
To define team-specific acronyms, project names, and internal terms that a new joiner would not know without context
To provide a dictionary of general programming terms
To list the third-party libraries used by the project
questions.explanation: Every team uses internal shorthand - project codenames, abbreviations, service nicknames. A glossary prevents new joiners from being blocked by unfamiliar terms in meetings and documentation.

questions.q: What does 'doc rot' refer to in documentation management?
options: Documentation that is too long and needs to be shortened
Documentation that has become inaccurate, outdated, or misleading because it was not updated as the system evolved
Documentation written in a language other than English
Documentation stored in the wrong location in Confluence or Notion
questions.explanation: Doc rot (documentation rot) is the decay of documentation accuracy over time. Outdated onboarding docs are particularly harmful because they waste new joiners' time and erode trust in documentation.

questions.q: Sarah posted this message in the #devs Slack channel after reviewing a PR: "This code doesn't use any of our preferred logging libraries. It also lacks clear error handling. Please update to follow the logging guidelines and add try/catch blocks for potential exceptions." B To provide a detailed walkthrough of the codebase and explain its functionality. B
C
D

Instead, she is pointing the developer to relevant existing documentation - the 'logging guidelines' - and highlighting the importance of adhering to established standards. This demonstrates how onboarding documentation should guide developers towards *where* to find information, rather than simply repeating technical details they likely already know. Option A is too broad; option D focuses on a specific task (debugging) rather than the broader goal of guiding adherence to best practices.

exercises.title: One-Pager Writing
exercises.subtitle: 4 exercises - write a one-pager / tech brief for leadership that is clear, concise, and persuasive within a 2-minute read.

questions.q: You are writing a one-pager to pitch a new engineering initiative to leadership, who will spend under 2 minutes reading it. Which opening line is correct?
options: "We propose investing 2 engineers for 6 weeks to migrate our CI pipeline to a faster runner, cutting average build time from 14 minutes to under 4 - saving ~40 engineer-hours/week across the org."
"This document discusses a proposal that our team has been considering for some time regarding potential improvements to our infrastructure."
"Background: our CI has been slow for a while and people complain about it."
"Let's talk about CI."
questions.explanation: A one-pager's opening line must deliver the ask, cost, and payoff in a single sentence - the "bottom line up front" (BLUF) principle. A busy executive should understand the entire proposal even if they read nothing else. Formula: "We propose [investment/ask] to [action], [quantified benefit] - [business impact]." Never open with throat-clearing ("this document discusses...") or vague background - a one-pager has no room for a slow build-up; every sentence must earn its place.

questions.q: Which structure correctly organises the body of a persuasive one-pager after the opening line?
options: A detailed 10-step technical implementation plan.
A single unbroken paragraph covering everything in chronological order.
Short labelled sections: Problem (with a number), Proposal (what/how), Cost (time/people/dollars), Impact (quantified benefit), and a clear Ask.
A list of every possible risk with no proposed solution.
questions.explanation: A one-pager should use short, labelled sections that a reader can scan in seconds - Problem, Proposal, Cost, Impact, Ask - each just a sentence or two. This is fundamentally different from a design doc or spec: the one-pager is a persuasion artifact for a non-implementing audience, not an implementation reference. Structure: "Problem: [quantified pain]. Proposal: [what we'll do]. Cost: [investment]. Impact: [expected result]. Ask: [specific decision requested - approval, budget, headcount]."

questions.q: The final section of a one-pager should be a clear "Ask." Which is correctly written?
options: "Ask: approval to allocate 2 engineers for 6 weeks starting next sprint. We need a decision by Friday to hit the Q3 roadmap."
"This is just for your information, no action needed."
"Let us know what you think."
"We'd appreciate any support you could offer."
questions.explanation: A one-pager exists to drive a decision, so the Ask must be specific and time-bound - exactly what is being requested (resources, approval, budget) and by when. Vague asks ("let us know what you think") produce no action and waste the document's purpose. Formula: "Ask: [specific decision/resource requested]. [Deadline or urgency, if applicable]." If the one-pager truly is FYI-only with no ask, say so explicitly ("No action needed - for awareness only") rather than leaving the reader unsure what's expected of them.

questions.q: A reviewer says your one-pager is "too technical for this audience." Which revision correctly addresses the feedback?
options: Add more technical detail to be thorough.
Remove all numbers and specifics, keep it vague.
Replace "we'll refactor the auth middleware to use JWT rotation with a 15-minute TTL" with "we'll upgrade our login security so that a stolen session token becomes useless within 15 minutes."
Add an appendix with the full architecture diagram to the one-pager itself.
questions.explanation: Adapting a one-pager for a non-technical audience means translating mechanism (JWT rotation, TTL) into outcome (what it means for security/risk) while keeping the concrete numbers that make the value tangible. This is not the same as removing all specificity - a good non-technical one-pager is still precise, just in outcome language rather than implementation language. Technique: for each technical term, ask "what does this mean for the reader's goals (cost, risk, speed, revenue)?" and lead with that translation; technical detail can move to a linked appendix, not the one-pager itself.

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I'm working on a new microservice to handle user profile updates. It uses Kafka for asynchronous processing and integrates with our existing database via gRPC. I've created a detailed API response schema and documented the gRPC calls in Swagger. (Attached: A draft PR description for this change)
options: A detailed API response schema is unnecessary for a PR description; developers can always consult the Swagger documentation later.
The PR description should prioritize a high-level overview of the changes, focusing on *what* the microservice does and *why* it's needed, rather than deep technical specifics.
It's best to include all technical details, like Kafka versions and gRPC method names, directly within the PR description to ensure clarity.
The PR description should only include a summary of the code changes, omitting any references to external integrations or protocols.
questions.explanation: This scenario reflects a common situation during code reviews. The goal of a PR description is to quickly inform reviewers about the *purpose* and *impact* of the change, not to provide exhaustive technical documentation. Including overly detailed information can overwhelm reviewers and slow down the process; instead, focus on the value proposition and how it relates to the broader system. Remember: One-pagers are meant for concise communication, prioritizing key elements over granular details.

questions.q: John : "Hey team, I've drafted a one-pager outlining the proposed migration to PostgreSQL for our analytics database. It includes estimated downtime, potential rollback strategies, and performance benchmarks based on similar migrations we've done in the past. I think it clearly communicates the benefits and risks ."
options: insufficient - the one-pager doesn't include a section detailing the impact on existing reporting dashboards.
correct - the statement reflects a confident understanding of the document's purpose and key information.
incorrect - the phrasing is too subjective; it should focus on quantifiable results rather than personal opinions.
incorrect - the one-pager needs to explicitly state the potential cost savings associated with the migration.
questions.explanation: This question assesses understanding of a key goal for documentation: objectivity. While John's enthusiasm is understandable, a one-pager intended for stakeholders needs to present information in a factual and measurable way. The 'correct' option acknowledges the document's purpose-clearly communicating benefits and risks-rather than relying on subjective assessment. Options B, C, and D all highlight areas where the statement lacks the necessary focus for effective communication.

questions.q: David : "Hey team, I'm submitting a PR for the new authentication service. It's heavily reliant on JWTs and uses Redis for caching. The API documentation is in OpenAPI format, and I've included some example usage scenarios within the PR description itself. I wanted to keep it concise - around 3-4 paragraphs max."
options: correct - brevity is key when documenting APIs, especially for quick reviews.
insufficient - the PR lacks a clear summary of the changes and their impact.
incorrect - including example scenarios in the PR description is unnecessary and adds to the complexity.
incorrect - OpenAPI documentation should be linked externally, not embedded within the PR itself.
questions.explanation: The core principle of a good one-pager (and PR description) is clarity and conciseness. David's approach-keeping it to 3-4 paragraphs-is appropriate for a quick review. While example scenarios are helpful, embedding them directly in the PR description can make it overly dense and harder to scan quickly. The key is to prioritize a clear summary of changes and their impact, which this response achieves.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'This one-pager is great! However, I noticed you've focused heavily on the technical details of the new logging service - the specifics of the log format and the implementation of the agent. For this audience (product managers and marketing), they need to understand *why* we're doing this and what the key benefits are. Can you revise it to highlight the business impact more prominently?'
options: Insufficient - the document only lists technical specifications.
The document is perfectly balanced, providing both technical detail and business context.
Too focused on implementation details ; the audience requires a high-level overview of the service's value and business goals.
Correct - the detailed technical information is crucial for developers reviewing the code.
questions.explanation: This question tests your understanding of tailoring documentation to different audiences. The reviewer's feedback indicates a common mistake: prioritizing technical specifics over the broader business justification. A one-pager aimed at stakeholders needs to clearly articulate the 'why' - what problem are we solving, and what value are we delivering? Option 2 incorrectly prioritizes the technical details; instead, focus on highlighting the benefits for the intended audience.

Including overly detailed information can overwhelm reviewers and slow down the process; instead, focus on the value proposition and how it relates to the broader system. Remember: One-pagers are meant for concise communication, prioritizing key elements over granular details.

questions.q: John : "Hey team, I've drafted a one-pager outlining the proposed migration to PostgreSQL for our analytics database. It includes estimated downtime, potential rollback strategies, and performance benchmarks based on similar migrations we've done in the past. I think it clearly communicates the benefits and risks ."
options: insufficient - the one-pager doesn't include a section detailing the impact on existing reporting dashboards.
correct - the statement reflects a confident understanding of the document's purpose and key information.
incorrect - the phrasing is too subjective; it should focus on quantifiable results rather than personal opinions.
incorrect - the one-pager needs to explicitly state the potential cost savings associated with the migration.
questions.explanation: This question assesses understanding of a key goal for documentation: objectivity. While John's enthusiasm is understandable, a one-pager intended for stakeholders needs to present information in a factual and measurable way. The 'correct' option acknowledges the document's purpose-clearly communicating benefits and risks-rather than relying on subjective assessment. incorrect - including example scenarios in the PR description is unnecessary and adds to the complexity.
insufficient - the PR lacks a clear summary of the changes and their impact.

exercises.title: Blameless Post-Mortem Writing
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - impact statements, blameless timelines, Five Whys root cause, action items with owners, and lessons learned. The SRE culture vocabulary.

questions.q: A post-mortem impact statement reads: "The payment system was down and lots of users were affected." A tech lead says it needs to be rewritten. Which version is better?
options: The payments service experienced an outage affecting customers.
Users reported issues with payments. The system was restored after some time.

On 2026-04-05 from 14:32 to 16:15 UTC (103 minutes), the payments service was unavailable. Approximately 14,800 checkout attempts failed. Estimated revenue impact: $87,000. 230 customer support tickets were opened.
All users were unable to pay for anything from 14:32 to 16:15 UTC on 2026-04-05.
questions.explanation: A strong impact statement answers four questions with specific, measurable data : 1. When? "2026-04-05 from 14:32 to 16:15 UTC" - exact timestamps, always in UTC 2. How long? "103 minutes" - duration, not just start/end 3. Who was affected and how? "14,800 checkout attempts failed" - not "lots of users" 4. What was the business impact? "Estimated revenue $87,000; 230 support tickets" - quantifies the cost Why specificity matters: Post-mortems are used to: • Prioritise which systems to improve first (high impact → high priority) • Report to stakeholders who need numbers, not impressions • Set a baseline for future incidents ("was this worse than last time?") • Drive SLO and error budget conversations Post-mortem impact vocabulary: "The outage lasted [N minutes/hours] from [start UTC] to [end UTC]." "Approximately [N] users / transactions / requests were affected." "Estimated revenue impact: [amount]." "[N] support tickets / customer complaints were received." "[Service X] was fully unavailable / degraded at [N]% reduced capacity."

questions.q: A post-mortem timeline entry reads: "14:47 - John noticed the error rate going up and eventually decided to check the database." A reviewer says this is not blameless enough. The improved version is _____.
options: "14:47 - John should have noticed the error rate sooner and acted faster."
"14:47 - The team failed to respond quickly enough to the error rate alert."
"14:47 - John noticed the error. He checked the database eventually."
"14:47 - Error rate observed at 12% (up from baseline 0.1%) in Datadog. On-call engineer initiated database health check."
questions.explanation: Blameless post-mortems focus on systems, signals, and decisions - not on people and their shortcomings. This is one of the most important concepts in SRE culture (pioneered by Google). What makes the corrected version blameless: • Names a system-level observable : "Error rate at 12% (up from baseline 0.1%)" • Uses a role rather than a name: "On-call engineer" - the individual isn't blamed; the system's response is tracked • Describes an action , not a judgment: "initiated database health check" • Could not be added to a performance review as evidence of failure Blameless writing vocabulary: "[Role/system] observed [metric] at [value] in [tool]." "The monitoring alert for [condition] did not fire." (system gap, not person gap) "The runbook did not cover this failure mode." (documentation gap) "At the time, the available information suggested [explanation] - leading to [decision]." Blameful vs. blameless rewrites: ❌ "Bob deployed without testing." → ✅ "The deployment pipeline did not require a staging test pass." ❌ "Alice missed the alert." → ✅ "The alert was not configured for the affected service." ❌ "The team took too long." → ✅ "Detection time was 34 minutes; alert threshold was set to 15 minutes delay."

questions.q: A post-mortem lists "Root Cause" as: "A bug in the payment service caused the outage." A senior SRE says this is incomplete. What is missing?
options: The "Five Whys" analysis - repeated "why" questions to find the systemic cause, not just the proximate technical fault
The git commit hash where the bug was introduced
The name of the developer who wrote the bug
A list of all services that were affected by the bug
questions.explanation: "A bug caused the outage" is never the root cause in a blameless post-mortem. It's the proximate cause - the immediate trigger. The root cause is the systemic condition that allowed the bug to reach production and cause an outage. The Five Whys applied: 1. Why did the outage happen? → The payment service crashed. 2. Why did it crash? → A null pointer exception on a required field. 3. Why did code with a null pointer exception reach production? → Unit tests didn't cover nil input on that path. 4. Why didn't tests cover that path? → Test coverage was below 60% for that module. 5. Why was coverage that low? → The service was migrated from Python 2 three years ago and tests were never backfilled. Root cause: "Insufficient test coverage on the payment service, a legacy of the Python 2 migration, allowed a nil-input regression to ship undetected." Post-mortem root cause vocabulary: "The proximate cause was X. The root cause was Y." "Five Whys analysis revealed that the underlying systemic issue was…" "Contributing factors included: …" "This failure mode was possible because [systemic gap]."

questions.q: The "Action Items" section of a post-mortem lists: "Fix the bug. Improve monitoring. Update documentation." A tech lead says these are unacceptable. Why?
options: Each action item must have: a specific owner, a due date, and a measurable success criterion - vague action items are never implemented
Action items should be listed as recommendations, not requirements
Action items belong in a separate JIRA ticket, not in the post-mortem document
There are too many action items - a post-mortem should have a maximum of two
questions.explanation: Vague post-mortem action items are one of the most common reasons incidents repeat. "Fix the bug" assigns no one, sets no deadline, and has no success criterion. What a complete action item requires: • Owner: one named person or team - not "the team" or "DevOps" • Due date: specific date, not "soon" or "next sprint" • What exactly: specific, measurable change • Priority: P1/P2 or equivalent - links to the incident's severity Rewritten action items: ❌ "Fix the bug." → ✅ "Add nil-safety checks to payment processor inputs. Owner: Maria G. Due: 2026-04-12." ❌ "Improve monitoring." → ✅ "Add Datadog alert for payment service error rate > 1% sustained for 2 minutes. Owner: SRE team. Due: 2026-04-10." ❌ "Update documentation." → ✅ "Update payments runbook with nil-input failure mode and recovery steps. Owner: Alex T. Due: 2026-04-15." Post-mortem action item vocabulary: "Action item: [specific task]. Owner: [name]. Priority: P[N]. Due: [date]. Success criterion: [measurable outcome]." "This is a preventive action." / "This is a detective action." / "This is a corrective action."

questions.q: A post-mortem document ends with: "We apologise to our users for the inconvenience caused." A senior engineer objects to this in an internal post-mortem. Why?
options: An internal post-mortem is a technical learning document - apologies belong in public-facing communications, not inside technical analysis. The post-mortem should end with lessons learned and action items.
The apology is too vague - it should specify which users were affected
Post-mortems should never acknowledge user impact in any form
Apologies are not professional in technical documents
questions.explanation: Different document types serve different purposes and audiences - and tone/content should match. Internal post-mortem: • Audience: engineers, SREs, tech leads • Purpose: understand what happened, prevent recurrence • Ending: lessons learned + action items with owners • Tone: analytical, neutral, forward-looking • No apologies, marketing language, or customer service tone Customer-facing incident communication: • Audience: users, customers • Purpose: acknowledge impact, explain what happened in non-technical terms, restore confidence • Includes: apology, impact acknowledgment, what was fixed, what prevents recurrence • Tone: empathetic, professional, clear Standard internal post-mortem closing sections: • "Lessons Learned / What Went Well / What Could Be Improved" - three lists • "Action Items" - the decisions made • "Review date" - when this post-mortem will be reviewed for progress Lessons Learned vocabulary: "What went well: Our oncall rotation detected the issue within [time]." "What could be improved: Our runbook did not cover this failure mode." "Key lesson: [systemic insight that applies beyond this incident]."

questions.q: PR#1234 has just been merged. During the code review of this PR, a junior developer, Maria, commented: 'This function is really complex and hard to understand. I think we need to add more comments.' The tech lead, David, responds with: 'That's good feedback, Maria. Let's document this clearly for future developers.' Which of the following best describes David's approach to post-mortem documentation related to this code?
options: C) Acknowledge Maria's feedback regarding complexity and commit to improving the overall clarity through targeted documentation-specifically outlining the function's purpose, inputs, and outputs-as part of a broader post-mortem reflection on code maintainability.
A) Focus solely on technical details about the function's implementation, including line-by-line explanations and complex algorithms.
B) Prioritize creating detailed comments within the code itself to address Maria's concern about understandability, regardless of existing documentation practices.
D) Dismiss Maria's comment as unnecessary detail, arguing that the code is self-explanatory and doesn't require additional comments or documentation to be effective.
questions.explanation: David's response demonstrates a blameless post-mortem mindset by recognizing the feedback while framing it within a larger context of improving future development. Option B is too granular and misses the point of a post-mortem; focusing solely on implementation details isn't the goal. Option C emphasizes adding comments *within* the code, which isn't always the most effective approach - clear documentation outside the code often provides better maintainability. Option A aligns with the purpose of a post-mortem: to identify areas for improvement and prevent future issues by documenting not just *what* the code does but *why* it was designed that way, contributing to overall understanding and reducing the risk of errors.

questions.q: During a post-mortem for an API outage caused by incorrect rate limiting, the team discusses documenting the changes made. Liam suggests: 'Let's write a detailed description of how the rate limits were adjusted and why.' Meanwhile, Chloe proposes: 'We should focus on recording the impact - how many requests were blocked, what services were affected, and the user experience metrics.' Which approach best aligns with the principles of blameless post-mortems?
options: redundant - we've already identified the root cause…
insufficient - the account balance is too low…
misleading - focusing solely on impact obscures the technical decisions made during the incident…
incomplete - it neglects to address the systemic issues that contributed to the problem…
questions.explanation: Liam's approach emphasizes documenting the *technical* changes, which is vital for future understanding and preventing recurrence. Chloe's response, while important to note the impact, doesn't address the underlying reasons for the rate limiting issue or the decisions made - a key element of blameless post-mortems. The goal is to understand *why* something happened, not just *what* happened and its consequences.

questions.q: A team is conducting a post-mortem on a recent deployment that resulted in intermittent performance issues. During the discussion, Emily suggests documenting the specific configuration changes made to the server as part of the post-mortem. Ben counters with: 'Let's focus on *what* happened - specifically, the spike in CPU usage and the corresponding impact on response times.' Which statement best reflects a blameless post-mortem approach?
options: Detailed technical documentation should be created separately after the post-mortem concludes, ensuring that the immediate discussion remains focused solely on identifying the cause of the incident.
Focusing on *what* happened - the observed symptoms and their impact - allows the team to identify the underlying issue without assigning blame or dwelling on specific actions.
Prioritizing documentation of configuration changes is crucial for future deployments and troubleshooting, even if it doesn't directly address the current problem.
The team should meticulously document every technical detail, regardless of its immediate relevance to understanding the root cause.
questions.explanation: Blameless post-mortems prioritize understanding *what* happened and its impact over assigning responsibility for individual actions. While documenting configuration changes is important for future deployments, it's not the primary focus during an immediate problem investigation. The core goal is to learn from the event and prevent similar issues, which requires a clear description of the observed symptoms and their consequences - option 2 accurately captures this.

questions.q: A team is investigating a recent incident where a new feature introduced intermittent errors in the user dashboard. During the post-mortem, Alex suggests documenting the specific code changes made to implement the feature, including commit hashes and associated tests. Ben argues that the focus should be on understanding *why* the errors occurred - specifically, the interactions between the new feature and existing components. Which of the following best represents a blameless post-mortem approach in this situation?
options: A: Prioritize documenting code changes to ensure traceability and facilitate future debugging efforts.
B: Focus solely on identifying the root cause of the errors, regardless of the specific implementation details.
C: Balance documentation of the code changes with a thorough investigation into the underlying causes and interactions, aiming for a holistic understanding.
D: Immediately revert the feature to its previous state to eliminate the errors, minimizing any disruption to users.
questions.explanation: The core principle of blameless post-mortems is not just about documenting *what* happened but *why*. While tracking code changes (A) and immediate rollback (D) are valid actions, they don't address the underlying systemic issues. Option C correctly balances both aspects - a comprehensive understanding necessitates recording the implementation details alongside a deep dive into the root cause and how the feature interacted with the existing system. This allows for preventative measures to be put in place.
