exercises.title: RFC & Design Documents
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - RFC openings, alternatives considered, trade-offs, open questions, and implementation plans. The structure and vocabulary that drives technical consensus.

questions.q: An engineer is writing the opening section of an RFC. Which opening best serves the document's purpose?
options: This RFC proposes a new approach to caching. The author believes the current approach is wrong and should be replaced immediately.
This is a document about Redis and caching. Please read it and let me know your thoughts.

This RFC proposes replacing our current per-service Redis instances with a shared Redis Cluster. The motivation is to reduce infrastructure cost by ~$4,200/month and eliminate 3 separate on-call failure modes while maintaining <5ms p99 cache latency.
As you all know, our current caching setup has many problems. I have a solution.
questions.explanation: An effective RFC opening must answer three questions in the first paragraph : 1. What is being proposed? "replacing per-service Redis instances with a shared Redis Cluster" 2. Why? "reduce cost by ~$4,200/month and eliminate 3 on-call failure modes" 3. What is the constraint/success criterion? "while maintaining <5ms p99 cache latency" This matters because senior engineers and stakeholders will read the title + first paragraph and decide whether to read further. If your opening is vague, persuasive, or personal-opinion-heavy, you lose credibility immediately. RFC opening anti-patterns: • "The author believes…" - RFCs make proposals, not personal arguments • "As you all know…" - assumes shared context, signals lazy writing • "Please read and let me know" - RFCs drive decisions, not open polls • No numbers - quantify the problem whenever possible Standard RFC sections: • Abstract / Summary • Motivation / Problem Statement • Proposal / Design • Alternatives Considered • Trade-offs / Drawbacks • Open Questions • Implementation Plan

questions.q: An RFC section is titled "Alternatives Considered." An engineer writes: "We considered using Memcached but rejected it." The section is weak. The most important improvement is to _____.
options: Add more alternatives - never stop at just one
Remove the section entirely - only one approach needs to be proposed
Move this section to the end of the document
Explain WHY each alternative was rejected - what specific trade-off, constraint, or requirement made it unsuitable for this particular case
questions.explanation: The "Alternatives Considered" section is often the most valuable part of an RFC - and the most commonly written poorly. What weak alternatives sections look like: "We considered X but decided against it." → completely useless "We considered X but it didn't work." → vague and unconvincing What strong alternatives sections look like: "We considered Memcached as an alternative to Redis Cluster. Memcached would reduce operational complexity (simpler data model) but it lacks Redis's support for sorted sets and pub/sub, which our leaderboard and invalidation features require. Additionally, Memcached does not support persistence - a hard requirement from the DBA team." Why this matters: • It shows you thought deeply about the problem - not just the first solution you found • It prevents readers from raising alternatives in review that you've already considered • It documents the trade-off reasoning for future engineers who will ask "why didn't they just use X?" • It builds trust: reviewers can see your reasoning, not just your conclusion The number of alternatives is less important than the depth of reasoning for each one.

questions.q: In an RFC's "Trade-offs" or "Drawbacks" section, an engineer writes: "This proposal has no significant drawbacks." A senior engineer says this is a red flag. Why?
options: The section should be titled "Risks" not "Drawbacks"
Every engineering decision has trade-offs - claiming none exist suggests the author either hasn't thought deeply enough or is hiding risks
This is fine if the proposal is simple enough
RFCs should only have a "Benefits" section, not a drawbacks section
questions.explanation: "No significant drawbacks" is one of the most reliable signals that an RFC hasn't been thought through carefully enough. Every engineering decision has trade-offs. Examples of real trade-offs to acknowledge: • Increased complexity - "This adds a new service dependency" • Operational overhead - "The team needs training on the new tool" • Migration cost - "Migrating 40 services to the new API will take ~3 sprints" • Performance in edge cases - "Under extreme load >10k RPS this approach adds 2ms latency" • Vendor dependency - "We become dependent on Vendor X's support and pricing" • Reversibility - "This migration is not easily reversible" Why acknowledging drawbacks builds trust: Readers know trade-offs exist. If you pretend they don't, readers assume you're either naive or selling something. Acknowledging limitations honestly demonstrates intellectual honesty and makes reviewers more likely to approve the proposal. RFC vocabulary for drawbacks: "The primary trade-off is…" "One limitation of this approach is…" "This introduces a potential risk of…" "The migration cost is estimated at…" "We accept this trade-off because…"

questions.q: An RFC includes a section titled "Open Questions." An engineer asks: "Why list things we don't know yet - doesn't that weaken the proposal?" What is the correct answer?
options: Open Questions weaken proposals and should be resolved before publishing the RFC
Open Questions are only included in external public RFCs, not internal design documents
Open Questions are a checklist of things the author plans to research next week
Open Questions explicitly surface unresolved decisions to invite community input - they invite reviewers to contribute expertise and prevent the RFC from blocking on unknown dependencies
questions.explanation: The "Open Questions" section is a deliberate and valuable tool in RFC writing, not a sign of weakness. What Open Questions achieve: • Surface decisions that are genuinely unknown or contested - instead of hiding them • Invite reviewers with specific expertise to contribute ("I know the answer to Q3") • Set expectations: "This RFC is approved in principle pending resolution of Q1 and Q2" • Prevent the author from being the single bottleneck on all unknowns Good open question examples: "Should the cluster use 3 or 5 replica shards? We recommend 3 for cost, but the DBA team should validate." "What SLA does the payments team require for cache misses? We need this to finalise the timeout configuration." "Is the security team comfortable with shared Redis for PII-adjacent data? Requires sign-off." Bad open question examples: "How does Redis work?" (research question, not a decision) "Should we do this?" (the RFC itself answers that) RFC vocab for open questions: "This remains an open question pending input from…" "We have not yet determined whether…" "This decision is deferred to…" "Feedback needed: …"

questions.q: A tech lead reads an RFC and leaves this comment: "The proposal is technically sound but the RFC doesn't address the implementation plan ." What is missing?
options: The RFC needs a phased rollout plan with milestones, owners, dependencies, and success metrics - so approval leads to a clear execution path, not another meeting to plan the plan
The RFC needs a list of sprint tickets broken down by story points
The RFC needs a Gantt chart showing the full project timeline
The RFC needs a code review checklist
questions.explanation: An RFC that lacks an implementation plan creates a common failure mode: it gets approved, then the team spends weeks figuring out how to actually execute it. What a strong RFC implementation plan includes: Phases: "Phase 1: Migrate 3 low-traffic services (Week 1-2). Phase 2: Migrate payments service (Week 3, requires Redis Cluster stable). Phase 3: Switch off old instances (Week 4)." Owners: "Infrastructure migration: Platform team. Service-level changes: individual service owners." Dependencies: "Phase 2 cannot start until Redis Cluster passes load testing." Success metrics: "Cache hit rate ≥ 85%, p99 latency < 5ms, zero failed migrations." Rollback plan: "If p99 latency exceeds 8ms, revert service-level connection strings to per-service Redis." RFC implementation vocabulary: "This will be rolled out in N phases, with phase 1 targeting…" "Phase 2 is gated on [condition]." "The rollback procedure is: …" "Success will be measured by: …" "Ownership: [team] is responsible for [scope]."

options: Focuses solely on the endpoint itself - it neglects to mention any related dependencies or potential impact.
Lacks clarity on required parameters - the description doesn't specify which fields are mandatory for updates.
Insufficient detail about error handling - users need to know what happens if something goes wrong.
Overly informal tone - a PR description should be professional and precise, not conversational.
questions.explanation: The primary issue is the lack of clarity regarding required parameters. A good API documentation PR description needs to explicitly state which fields are mandatory for updates; otherwise, developers won't know how to correctly call the endpoint and could lead to errors or unexpected behavior. While the other options touch on aspects of good documentation (error handling, tone), defining required parameters is a core element for usability and reducing support requests. Sarah 's message prioritizes brevity over precise information, which is often detrimental in code reviews and API consumption.

questions.q: David : 'Hey team, I'm writing the PR description for this new feature. We're exposing a GraphQL endpoint that allows clients to fetch aggregated data based on various filters. The current draft says: 'New endpoint added - fetches data!' What's the most crucial addition to make this description more effective and aligned with RFC best practices? Options:
options: Add a link to the relevant RFC document for further details.
Clearly state the expected response format (schema) of the GraphQL endpoint, including data types and potential errors.
Include a summary of the technical design choices made for the endpoint's query structure.
Provide a brief explanation of the filters supported by the endpoint and their impact on performance.
questions.explanation: The primary goal of an RFC and its associated PR description is to provide technical clarity. Option 1 addresses this directly by explaining the design choices - crucial for developers understanding how the endpoint functions and its limitations. Options 2, 3, and 4 are important but secondary; a developer needs to know *how* the data is structured and filtered before delving into performance or simply referencing the RFC. A good PR description should clearly communicate the technical details of the change.

questions.q: Mark is reviewing a draft RFC for a new service. He finds the section on 'Future Enhancements' reads: 'This initial release will support basic authentication and data validation. Future enhancements may include multi-factor authentication and integration with third-party identity providers.' Mark comments, 'This feels a little vague. It doesn't give us much to go on for future development.' Which of the following responses is MOST appropriate for Mark to offer to the author?
options: Insufficient - the RFC lacks specific technical details about potential future enhancements.
Correct - The section should provide a high-level overview of anticipated features and their potential impact, not just a list of possibilities.
Acceptable - Future enhancements are inherently uncertain, and this level of detail is sufficient for initial planning.
Too detailed - the RFC needs to focus solely on the current scope, avoiding speculation about future development.
questions.explanation: The key here is understanding that an 'Future Enhancements' section in an RFC shouldn't be a speculative wishlist. It should outline *potential* directions for the service, but with enough clarity to inform architectural decisions and prioritization. Option 1 correctly identifies this by pointing out the lack of concrete details - it needs more than just stating possibilities; it requires discussing potential impacts and considerations. Options B, C, and D either misunderstand the purpose of that section or suggest a level of detail inappropriate for an early-stage RFC.

questions.q: During a code review, Liam points out an RFC draft for a new payment processing system. He notes the 'Known Limitations' section states: 'The initial implementation will only support Visa and Mastercard transactions. Support for other card types will be added in a later release.' Another reviewer, Maya, suggests adding a sentence to the section about potential impacts on existing systems. Liam replies: 'Let's not over-engineer this now - it's just a small payment system.' What is the *primary* reason Maya's suggestion is valuable?
options: It adds unnecessary technical detail that won't be relevant for the initial implementation, potentially confusing future developers.
It proactively addresses potential risks and dependencies by acknowledging how the new system might affect existing infrastructure - a critical consideration for any integration.
It clarifies the scope of the project and sets expectations for future development, ensuring alignment with overall business goals.
It forces the author to immediately commit to supporting all major card types, accelerating the development timeline and minimizing potential delays.
questions.explanation: The correct answer highlights the importance of considering dependencies and impacts. While Liam's focus on a 'small payment system' is understandable, neglecting to document potential integration challenges in an RFC can lead to significant problems later. The 'Known Limitations' section should proactively address how this new system might interact with existing systems - this is crucial for risk mitigation and future development planning. Option A focuses on unnecessary detail; options B, C, and D misinterpret the purpose of the limitations section.

questions.q: Alex is drafting an RFC for a new caching layer. He includes a section titled 'Performance Metrics.' Alex writes: 'Initial tests show a 20% reduction in API latency during peak load.' During a code review, his team lead asks, 'That's good, but what specific metrics are we tracking and how do they relate to our SLAs? How will we *prove* this improvement?' Which of the following is the MOST effective response Alex could offer to address his team lead's concerns?
options: 'We tracked average request time and found a 20% decrease, which meets our internal benchmarks.'
'We've defined key metrics like 99th percentile latency and are monitoring them against our Service Level Agreements (SLAs). We'll provide detailed reports on these metrics.'
'We're just using latency as a proxy for performance. It's good enough.'
'Let's just stick with the initial results; further testing would take too long.'
questions.explanation: The incorrect options demonstrate a lack of rigor and a failure to consider operational requirements. Option C dismisses important performance considerations. Option A focuses on internal benchmarks without connecting them to external SLAs. Option D suggests abandoning thorough investigation. Option B highlights the crucial step of defining measurable metrics tied directly to Service Level Agreements, demonstrating a commitment to quantifiable improvement and providing evidence for ongoing monitoring - precisely what the team lead requested.

exercises.title: Runbook Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practice runbook vocabulary: prerequisites sections, numbered procedures, decision trees, review dates, and runbook accuracy testing.

questions.q: A runbook template starts with 'a prerequisites section.' What should this section contain?
options: A summary of the incident

Everything the on-call engineer needs before starting: required access (VPN, AWS role), tools to install, background knowledge to have, and any conditions that must be true before the procedure starts
A list of team contacts
The history of past incidents
questions.explanation: The prerequisites section prevents the on-call engineer from getting halfway through a runbook and discovering they lack access or a required tool. It lists everything needed upfront: permissions, CLI tools, environment setup, and pre-conditions - saving critical time during incidents.

questions.q: Your runbook uses 'numbered steps for the procedure.' Why is numbered formatting important?
options: Numbered steps are required by compliance frameworks
Numbered steps allow the engineer to track progress under stress, communicate clearly ('I'm on step 7'), and return to the right place after an interruption - critical during high-pressure incidents
Numbered steps make the runbook shorter
Only engineers with senior titles can use numbered procedures
questions.explanation: During incidents, engineers are under pressure and may be handling multiple communications. Numbered steps provide clear position tracking ('done through step 5'), enable handoff between engineers ('pick up from step 8'), and reduce the cognitive load of tracking where you are in the procedure.

questions.q: An advanced runbook includes 'a decision tree that guides the on-call engineer.' When is a decision tree more useful than a linear list of steps?
options: When the runbook has more than 10 steps
When the procedure has conditional branches - e.g., 'If metric X is above threshold, go to step 5; otherwise go to step 12' - a decision tree maps these branches clearly
Decision trees are only for network troubleshooting
When the team is too large for linear procedures
questions.explanation: Decision trees shine when the procedure diverges based on observed conditions. A linear runbook handles this awkwardly with 'if/else' prose; a visual or structured decision tree makes the branching obvious, reduces errors, and is faster to follow under pressure.

questions.q: A runbook header says 'Last reviewed: 2024-01-15.' Why does the review date matter?
options: It is a legal requirement

Runbooks become outdated as systems evolve - the review date signals how current the procedure is. Stale runbooks give wrong instructions during real incidents. Regular reviews ensure the procedure matches the current system state
Review dates affect runbook search ranking
The date is only relevant for compliance audits
questions.explanation: Runbooks that are never reviewed become dangerous - systems change, services are renamed or retired, credentials expire, and procedures evolve. The review date helps the on-call engineer assess how much to trust the runbook and flags runbooks that need updating. Many teams require quarterly reviews.

questions.q: Your team says 'The runbook test verifies the steps are accurate.' What does runbook testing involve?
options: Asking a developer to read the runbook
Executing the runbook procedure in a staging or game day environment to confirm every step works as written - finding gaps, outdated commands, or missing context before an actual incident
Reviewing the runbook in a team meeting
Automated syntax checking of the markdown
questions.explanation: Runbook testing (often done during game days or scheduled drills) involves actually executing the procedure to verify it works. This finds stale commands, missing environment setup, incorrect API endpoints, and confusing wording - ensuring the runbook is reliable before it's needed under pressure.

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I'm running this deployment for the new user authentication service. It's failing intermittently - I've checked the logs and nothing obvious stands out. Can someone review my runbook to see if I missed anything?" Which of the following is the MOST appropriate follow-up question you should ask Sarah to ensure a thorough runbook review, focusing on potential issues *before* she continues deploying?
options: insufficient - the account balance is too low...
incorrect - Sarah should immediately halt deployment and investigate the logs.
correct - Can you describe the specific steps you followed in the runbook leading up to the failure, and what data points you're monitoring during each step?
faulty - Sarah's request implies a complete failure, requiring immediate escalation.
questions.explanation: The correct answer focuses on understanding Sarah 's process within the runbook. Asking about the steps she followed and monitored forces her to articulate *how* she applied the documented procedures, revealing potential deviations or omissions that might be causing the intermittent failures. The other options are either too prescriptive (immediately halting), dismissive of the runbook's role, or incorrectly frame the situation - a failure isn't necessarily due to a missed step but could stem from unexpected data or environment variations.

questions.q: John : "I'm deploying a new feature to production. The runbook says to update the database schema version and restart the API service. I've done both, but the monitoring dashboard is showing high latency. Should I just roll it back?"
options: insufficient - the rollback procedure isn't clearly defined in the runbook.
correct - a high latency immediately after deployment suggests a critical issue requiring immediate rollback to prevent further disruption.

incorrect - before rolling back, John should first consult the runbook's troubleshooting section for common post-deployment issues and check if there are any related alerts or metrics that provide more context.
incorrect - high latency is normal during deployments; John should monitor the dashboard for a few minutes to see if it resolves itself.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights the importance of proactive troubleshooting within a runbook. Simply rolling back immediately might mask an underlying problem and prevent learning from the deployment. The correct answer emphasizes the need to consult the runbook's troubleshooting guidance first - which often includes expected metrics and potential alerts - before resorting to a rollback. It's crucial to understand *why* the issue occurred, not just react to the symptom.

questions.q: David : "I've drafted a PR description for this rollback. It says 'Rollback database schema to version 20231027 and restart the API service.' Seems straightforward enough."
options: insufficient - the PR description lacks details about monitoring checks.
correct - the PR description is concise and clearly outlines the steps.
redundant - a rollback runbook should include both schema version and service restart instructions automatically.
unnecessary - the deployment team will manually verify the database version before restarting the API.
questions.explanation: The PR description needs to be more than just a list of actions. While stating 'Rollback database schema to version 20231027 and restart the API service' is a good start, it doesn't include critical checks like verifying latency or ensuring downstream services are unaffected after the rollback. A robust PR description should explicitly mention these validation steps to prevent further issues during the recovery process; this ensures that the rollback isn't just a technical action but a deliberate attempt to restore stability.

questions.q: You're reviewing a runbook for a critical service outage. The runbook includes a section titled 'Rollback Actions'. Which of the following is the MOST crucial element to ensure a successful and safe rollback?
options: A: Detailed steps on how to manually trigger a full database restore from backups.
B: A clear list of dependencies that *must* be considered before initiating the rollback, including potential impact on dependent services and downstream systems.
C: Confirmation that all impacted users have been notified about the planned outage and its expected duration.
D: A simple command to automatically revert all code changes pushed to the main branch.
questions.explanation: The most critical aspect of a rollback action is understanding its potential impact. Option B highlights the need to consider dependencies - failing to do so can lead to cascading failures or data inconsistencies. Options A and D are too simplistic and don't address the complexities of a real-world rollback scenario; option C focuses on communication, which is important but secondary to preventing further damage during the process.

exercises.title: Runbook & Operational Procedures
exercises.subtitle: 5 exercises - trigger conditions, exact commands, verification steps, rollback procedures, and runbook maintenance. Write runbooks people can follow at 3am.

questions.q: An SRE is writing a runbook step for restarting the payments service. Which version is best for use at 3am during an incident?
options: Restart the payments service if it appears to be having issues.
If you think there might be a memory leak, consider possibly restarting the service after checking with the team.
Restart the payments service using kubectl as needed.

Run: kubectl rollout restart deployment/payments-service -n production - Expected: Pod restarts within 60 seconds. Verify: kubectl get pods -n production | grep payments should show all Pods in Running state. If Pods remain in CrashLoopBackOff after 2 minutes, escalate to the platform team (#platform-oncall).
questions.explanation: The best runbook step has five elements that allow a stressed engineer to follow it at 3am: 1. Exact command: No ambiguity about what to run. Copy-pasteable. 2. Expected outcome: "Pod restarts within 60 seconds" - the engineer knows what success looks like. 3. Verification step: A command to confirm the action worked. 4. Time expectation: "after 2 minutes" - so the engineer knows when to stop waiting. 5. Escalation path: Who to call if this step fails, and how to reach them. Runbook writing principles: • Write for someone who has never seen this service before • Use active, imperative verbs: Run, Verify, Check, Escalate - not "you might want to" • Never say "if appropriate" or "as needed" - these are decisions the runbook should make for the reader • Include rollback steps • Include links to dashboards and relevant logs Anti-patterns to avoid: ❌ "Fix the memory issue" (not actionable) ❌ "Check if there are problems" (too vague) ❌ "As per standard procedure" (circular reference to nothing)

questions.q: A runbook begins: "This runbook covers restarting the auth service." A senior SRE says it's incomplete. The critical missing element in the runbook's opening is _____.
options: A list of all team members who reviewed it
A description of WHEN to use this runbook - what symptoms, alerts, or conditions trigger its use
The expected downtime during the procedure
The author's name and last review date
questions.explanation: A runbook without a clear trigger condition is dangerous: engineers either use it when they shouldn't, or don't use it when they should. A complete runbook opening includes: Purpose: "This runbook describes how to restart the auth service." When to use: "Use when: (1) PagerDuty alert 'auth-service-high-latency' fires AND p99 latency > 500ms for 5+ minutes, OR (2) auth service Pods are in CrashLoopBackOff." Prerequisites: "Requires access to: production namespace, Datadog, #incidents-channel." Estimated duration: "~5 minutes if Pods restart normally; escalate if >15 minutes." Last tested: "2026-03-15 by Alice Chen" Why the trigger condition matters most: Engineers arriving at an incident are stressed. They need to know immediately: "Is this the right runbook for my situation?" Without explicit trigger conditions, they either apply the wrong runbook (causing additional damage) or waste time reading through to find out if it applies. Runbook metadata vocabulary: "This runbook applies when…" "Trigger conditions: …" "Do NOT use this runbook if…" "Prerequisites: the following access / tools are required: …"

questions.q: A runbook step says: "Scale up the consumer service." A new engineer is confused. Which rewritten step is clearest?
options: Run: kubectl scale deployment/consumer-service --replicas=10 -n production - this increases from the current replica count to 10. Verify consumer lag in Datadog dashboard [link] drops below 50,000 messages within 3 minutes.
The consumer service should be scaled. Increase replicas.
Scale up the consumer service to handle the load.
Increase the consumer-service to 10 replicas if needed.
questions.explanation: Good runbook steps always answer: exactly what action, with what value, how to verify success . Breaking down the correct answer: • Exact command: `kubectl scale deployment/consumer-service --replicas=10 -n production` - no guessing what "scale up" means • Context: "increases from the current replica count to 10" - the engineer knows what's changing • Verification: specific metric (consumer lag), specific threshold (50,000), specific tool (Datadog) with a link, specific timeframe (3 minutes) Why vague runbook steps cause incidents: "Scale up" → how many? 5? 20? 100? "If needed" → who decides when it's needed? During an incident, this becomes a debate "Handle the load" → not measurable - how do you know it's working? Runbook action verb vocabulary: • "Run:" - for commands • "Navigate to:" - for UI steps • "Verify that:" - for checks • "If [condition], then:" - for conditional steps • "Wait until:" - for waiting with a success criterion • "Escalate to [team] via [channel] if:" - for escalation triggers

questions.q: A runbook includes a section titled "Rollback Procedure." When should this section be used - and why is it essential?
options: Use it only if the entire production environment fails - it's a last resort
Use it after the incident is fully resolved to clean up temporary changes
Rollback procedures only apply to database migrations, not service restarts
Use it if any step in the runbook causes unexpected behaviour or makes the situation worse - the rollback procedure restores the system to its state before the runbook was applied
questions.explanation: A rollback procedure answers: "If following this runbook makes things worse, how do we undo what we just did?" Why rollback sections are essential: • Runbook actions sometimes have unexpected side effects • A configuration change applied under pressure might have been the wrong one • An engineer needs to know they can safely undo actions without escalating What a good rollback section looks like: "If after scaling to 10 replicas the consumer lag increases or error rate rises above 5%, roll back: kubectl scale deployment/consumer-service --replicas=3 -n production and notify #incidents with the current metrics." Key rollback vocabulary: "Revert this change by:" "To restore to the previous state:" "Undo [step N] by running:" "Check the previous replica count in Datadog before scaling down" "Tag this incident with [label] so the post-mortem covers the rollback" Rollback anti-patterns: ❌ "Undo the changes" (not actionable) ❌ No rollback section at all ❌ "Ask someone" (by 3am, "someone" may not be available) ❌ Rollback that requires the same expertise as the original fix

questions.q: After an engineer successfully follows a runbook to resolve an incident, they notice one of the steps was outdated and no longer matched the current Kubernetes namespace. What is the correct action regarding the runbook?
options: Delete the wrong step so future engineers don't follow it
Leave it as-is - every engineer should verify each step against current infrastructure anyway
Update the runbook immediately after the incident, note the date and your name, and flag the change in the team channel - runbooks that aren't maintained become dangerous
File a ticket for the documentation team to update it next quarter
questions.explanation: A runbook that isn't maintained becomes more dangerous over time than having no runbook at all - because it creates false confidence. Runbook maintenance vocabulary: "Update the runbook to reflect the current namespace/configuration." "Add a note: 'Updated 2026-04-07 - namespace changed from `legacy` to `production` (Alex T.).'" "Notify the team: 'Updated the auth restart runbook - step 3 namespace was wrong. Fixed.'" When to update runbooks: • After any incident where a step was wrong, unclear, or missing • After infrastructure changes (new namespace, new tool, changed service name) • After any "first use" - the person using a runbook for the first time always finds inaccuracies • On a regular review schedule (quarterly at minimum for critical runbooks) Runbook update best practices: • Add "Last tested by" and "Last updated" fields • Use version history or Git blame so teams can see what changed • Include who to contact if a step is unclear • Run fire drills: have a new team member follow the runbook and identify gaps The "blameless maintainer" principle: updating a runbook after finding an error is a contribution, not an admission of fault.

The PR description includes the following step: 'Update the API endpoint to reflect the latest schema.' A senior developer asks her to add more detail about the expected response format after the update. Which of the following additions would be most appropriate to include in the PR description, aligning with best practices for runbook documentation?
options: A general statement confirming that the developer will 'handle the details' of the update.
A link to the latest API schema document and a reminder to validate the response against it.
Detailed instructions on how to test the new API endpoint after the schema change.
Insufficient - only stating the endpoint update is technically correct but lacks context.
questions.explanation: The original description is insufficient because runbooks need *actionable* steps. While stating the endpoint change is technically correct, it doesn't provide the developer with what to do next or how to verify success. Option 2 directly addresses the senior developer's request for more detail by outlining a crucial testing step. It emphasizes validating the response against the updated schema - a standard practice in API documentation and runbook creation to ensure functionality after changes.

exercises.title: Technical Spec Writing
exercises.subtitle: 4 exercises - write technical specification documents with measurable requirements, clear scope boundaries, and explicit edge case handling.

questions.q: A technical specification's "Requirements" section should state what the system must do. Which requirement is correctly written?
options: "The API must respond within 200ms at the P95 percentile for GET requests under a load of 500 requests/second, with 99.9% availability measured monthly."
"We want the system to work well."
"The system should be fast and reliable."
"Performance is important for this feature."
questions.explanation: A specification requirement must be measurable and testable - a specific number, percentile, condition, and time window - so engineers can build to it and QA can verify it. "Fast and reliable" cannot be verified; a P95 latency target under a defined load can be. Formula: "[Component] must [specific measurable behaviour] under [defined condition], measured [how/when]." This is the core distinction between a spec and a design doc: a spec states the contract (what), while a design doc explains how it will be achieved.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly belongs in the "Non-Functional Requirements" section of a spec, as opposed to functional requirements?
options: "When a user clicks 'Submit', the form data is sent to the server."
"The dropdown must list all available countries."
"The login endpoint must accept an email and password and return a JWT token."
"The system must support 10,000 concurrent authenticated sessions and encrypt all data at rest using AES-256."
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements describe qualities of the system - scalability, security, performance, availability - rather than specific features/behaviours (which are functional requirements). "Support 10,000 concurrent sessions" and "encrypt at rest" are both cross-cutting system qualities, not individual features. Vocabulary: "functional requirement" (what the system does - a specific feature/behaviour), "non-functional requirement / quality attribute" (how well the system does it - performance, security, scalability, maintainability).

questions.q: A spec includes an "Out of Scope" section listing what the system will NOT do. Why is this section important, and which entry is correctly written?
options: "Out of Scope: bugs."
"Out of Scope: everything not mentioned above." (too vague to be useful)
Omit the section entirely - it's not necessary.
"Out of Scope: multi-currency support. This spec covers USD transactions only; multi-currency will be addressed in a follow-up spec (tracked in JIRA-4521)."
questions.explanation: An Out of Scope entry should name a specific capability that was considered but deliberately excluded, and ideally reference where it will be tracked. This prevents scope creep during implementation and manages stakeholder expectations up front - readers who need multi-currency support know immediately it's not covered here. Formula: "Out of Scope: [specific capability]. [Reason/context]. [Where it will be addressed, if applicable]."

questions.q: An engineer reviewing a spec asks: "What happens if the payment provider times out?" Which addition correctly handles this in the "Edge Cases" or "Error Handling" section?
options: "Timeouts shouldn't happen if the provider is reliable."

"If the payment provider does not respond within 10 seconds, the system must return a 504 to the client, log the timeout with the transaction ID, and place the transaction in a 'pending-retry' state for reconciliation - never silently mark it as failed or succeeded."
"We'll figure that out during implementation."
"Just retry a few times, that should work."
questions.explanation: Edge case / error handling entries in a spec must define the exact behaviour for failure conditions - response code, logging, and resulting state - because ambiguity here is exactly what causes production incidents (e.g. double-charging or silently lost transactions). Specs that skip edge cases push the decision to whoever implements it, under time pressure, without full context. Formula: "If [failure condition], the system must [exact behaviour], [logging/observability requirement], and [resulting state] - [explicit exclusion of dangerous behaviour]."

questions.q: Sarah is writing a PR description for a new API endpoint that calculates shipping costs. She wants to clearly communicate the expected behavior to her team. Which of the following descriptions best fulfills this purpose? Option A: 'This endpoint will return a JSON object with the total cost.' Option B: 'The function takes an order and returns the calculated shipping fee based on weight and destination.' Option C: 'This API call is for handling shipping. It's pretty simple.' Option D: 'The system calculates shipping costs; it's a core feature.'
options: 'The system calculates shipping costs; it's a core feature.'
'The function takes an order and returns the calculated shipping fee based on weight and destination.'
'This endpoint will return a JSON object with the total cost.'
'This API call is for handling shipping. It's pretty simple.'
questions.explanation: Option B provides the most specific and informative description of the endpoint's functionality. It clearly outlines the inputs (an order) and the expected output (the calculated shipping fee), referencing key technical details like weight and destination-crucial for developers to understand how to utilize the API. Options C is too vague, simply stating the return type; Option D lacks detail and isn't helpful for understanding the process, and Option A treats it as a generic feature without describing its technical implementation.

questions.q: David is reviewing a pull request for a new user authentication service. He sees the following draft PR description: "This endpoint handles user login and registration." As a senior developer, David notices this description lacks crucial detail. Which of the following options would be the MOST appropriate addition to ensure clarity during the code review?
options: Insufficient - the description doesn't specify authentication methods or security considerations.
Good, but it could be improved by mentioning the expected input data types and potential error handling scenarios.
Excellent! The description is concise and clearly outlines the primary function of the endpoint.
This is a perfectly acceptable initial description. Further clarification can be added later during the discussion.
questions.explanation: The original description is too vague for a code review. A good PR description needs to communicate not just *what* the endpoint does but also *how* it's intended to operate and any important considerations like security or potential errors. Option A highlights this crucial gap - failing to detail authentication methods or security protocols leaves room for misunderstandings. Options C and B are overly positive, while option D is complacent and doesn't address the need for a detailed description.

questions.q: Liam is drafting a PR description for a new feature that allows users to upload profile pictures. He's struggling to clearly articulate the expected behavior to his team. Below are four options he's considered. Which option best fits within a technical specification document, providing sufficient detail for reviewers? Context: A clear PR description should outline what the code *does*, not just what it *is*.
options: Option A: 'This feature allows users to upload profile pictures.'
Option B: 'The uploaded image will be resized and saved in the /images/users directory.'
Option C: 'This is a new user interface element for uploading images.'
Option D: 'This PR implements the profile picture upload functionality - further details are available in the associated task'
questions.explanation: The correct answer, Option B, provides concrete detail about what happens to the uploaded image. This is crucial for reviewers to understand the technical implementation and potential issues (like resizing). Options A is too vague, C focuses on UI rather than functionality, and D deflects responsibility by stating further details are elsewhere - a PR description should be self-contained enough to provide sufficient context. Liam needs to clearly communicate *how* the feature operates.

exercises.subtitle: Practice technical specification vocabulary: spec scope, review-before-implement, deviations, assumptions and constraints, and stakeholder sign-off.

questions.q: A team process says 'The technical spec covers design, API, and testing.' Why include all three in a single spec?
options: It makes the spec longer

Covering design (how it works), API (how it's exposed), and testing (how it's verified) in one document ensures alignment between implementation, interface, and quality expectations before any code is written
Design and testing should be separate documents
APIs don't need to be specified
questions.explanation: A comprehensive technical spec aligns the team on the full solution before implementation. Design covers internal structure; API covers external contracts; testing covers acceptance criteria. Together they ensure implementation, API consumers, and QA are aligned - preventing mismatches discovered after the code is written.

questions.q: Your team's process requires 'The spec is reviewed before implementation.' What is the benefit of reviewing before coding?
options: It delays the project unnecessarily
Review before implementation catches design flaws, identifies missing requirements, surfaces dependencies, and aligns stakeholders when changes are cheap - before the cost of implementation is sunk
Reviews are only useful after implementation
Pre-implementation review only works for large teams
questions.explanation: Changes to a spec are cheap - a comment and a document edit. Changes to implemented code are expensive - refactoring, testing, updating APIs. Pre-implementation review is the most cost-effective quality gate. It finds gaps, catches ambiguities, and surfaces concerns before any implementation investment is made.

questions.q: A spec note says 'The implementation may deviate from the spec if needed.' What should a developer do when they deviate?
options: Deviate silently and update the spec after shipping
Document the deviation in the spec with the reason - so the spec remains an accurate record of what was built and why it diverged from the original plan
Discard the spec once deviation occurs
Request a full re-review before deviating
questions.explanation: Deviating from the spec without documenting it creates a dangerous gap - the spec says one thing, the code does another, and future maintainers are misled. When deviation is necessary, update the spec to reflect the actual implementation and explain why the deviation was made.

questions.q: Your spec template includes 'assumptions and constraints.' What is the purpose of documenting assumptions?
options: Assumptions are obvious and don't need documentation
Documenting assumptions makes them explicit - other team members can challenge false assumptions before implementation, and future readers understand what the design depends on being true
Assumptions are documented only for security specs
Assumptions should be excluded to keep specs concise
questions.explanation: Undocumented assumptions are one of the most common causes of technical problems. 'We assumed the external API would always return in under 200ms' is a classic undocumented assumption that creates fragile systems. Documenting assumptions makes them challengeable and creates a checklist of things to verify.

questions.q: A spec process includes 'stakeholder sign-off.' Who are typical stakeholders for a technical spec sign-off?
options: Only the CEO

The engineers implementing the work, the team lead or architect reviewing technical soundness, product management confirming requirements, and sometimes security or infrastructure if their domains are affected
Only the product manager
Only senior engineers
questions.explanation: Stakeholder sign-off ensures all affected parties have reviewed and agreed to the plan. Technical specs typically involve: implementing engineers (confirming they understand and agree), a tech lead/architect (confirming technical soundness), product management (confirming requirements are met), and cross-functional partners whose systems are affected.

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I'm starting work on the new user authentication API. The spec says it should support OAuth 2.0 and JWT tokens. I'm thinking of just returning a simple JSON object with the user ID and email for the response." Mark (during a code review): "I noticed you're not explicitly stating the expected error responses in the spec. What if the authentication fails? Should we return a 401 Unauthorized or something else?"
options: Insufficient - simply returning user ID and email is sufficient for basic functionality.
Correct - adhering strictly to the spec is paramount, even if it requires more complex response formats.
Partially Correct - including error responses is important, but the core data (user ID & email) should always be present.
Incorrect - the spec only dictates the primary data structure; error handling details are the responsibility of the implementation team.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights a key aspect of technical specifications: clarity and completeness. While the spec outlines core requirements like OAuth 2.0 and JWT tokens, it doesn't dictate every detail of the response format. The correct answer acknowledges that error handling should be considered, but emphasizes that the foundational data (user ID & email) remains a necessary component. Options A and D miss this crucial point about defining complete responses, while option C oversimplifies the importance of error management.

questions.q: Mark is reviewing a pull request for a new feature. The PR description states: 'This API endpoint will return a list of products matching the search query.' However, during his review, Mark points out that the spec doesn't define what happens if no products are found. He asks, 'Should we include an error code in the response?' Which of the following is the MOST appropriate action for the developer to take regarding Mark 's comment?
options: Insufficient - the API description is perfectly clear and doesn't require additional details.
Immediately incorporate the suggested error handling, as it's a critical part of the API contract.
Clarify with Mark why he believes an error code is necessary. Perhaps there's a misunderstanding about the expected response format.
Ignore the comment; the PR description provides sufficient information for developers to understand how the endpoint should behave.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights the importance of API contracts and clear specifications. The correct answer emphasizes that an error code is a crucial component of a robust API response - it defines what happens under exceptional conditions. Options A and D suggest neglecting critical details, while option C focuses on questioning the *reasoning* behind the request, rather than addressing the core issue of defining error handling. Ignoring the comment (option B) would be a significant oversight, as proper error management is vital for API reliability.

questions.q: David : "I'm implementing the new payment processing API. The spec says 'All transactions must be logged with a timestamp and unique ID.' I'm just using `console.log` for now to debug. It's quick, right?"
options: insufficient - logging is not required by the specification.
acceptable - console logs are sufficient for debugging during development.
incorrect - the spec mandates a structured log format, not simple console output.
correct - console logs are an efficient way to capture transaction data.
questions.explanation: The technical specification clearly defines 'All transactions must be logged...'. `console.log` doesn't meet this requirement because it lacks a structured format (timestamp and unique ID). While useful for debugging, the spec dictates a formal logging mechanism to ensure data integrity and auditability. Using `console.log` bypasses this critical element.

questions.q: During a standup meeting, Maria says, 'I'm working on the user profile update endpoint. The spec outlines a GraphQL schema for retrieving data. I've decided to just use the REST API directly and return a JSON payload - it's simpler.' What is Maria primarily overlooking?
options: the importance of adhering to agreed-upon architectural patterns.
potential inconsistencies between the GraphQL schema and the underlying data model.
the need for thorough documentation of the new endpoint's functionality.
the risk of creating technical debt due to a deviation from the specification.
questions.explanation: While simplicity can be valuable, a technical specification often defines *how* the API should interact with the system. Directly using the REST API and returning a JSON payload without aligning with the specified GraphQL schema introduces risk - potentially creating inconsistencies and contributing to technical debt. Following the spec ensures interoperability and maintainability.

exercises.title: Internal Wiki and Knowledge Base Writing (English)
exercises.subtitle: Practice the vocabulary and best practices for writing internal wikis and knowledge bases: structure, discoverability, and maintenance.

questions.q: What distinguishes a 'knowledge base' from a 'wiki' in a corporate context?
options: Knowledge bases use Confluence; wikis use Notion
A knowledge base is typically curated and structured for specific use cases (e.g., support articles, FAQs); a wiki is more open and collaborative with less editorial control
Knowledge bases are for customers; wikis are for engineers only
There is no difference - the terms are interchangeable
questions.explanation: While often used interchangeably, knowledge bases typically have more structure and editorial oversight (especially customer-facing ones). Wikis tend to be open, collaborative, and grow organically.

questions.q: What is a 'single source of truth' (SSOT) in documentation strategy?
options: Storing all documentation in a single file
Designating one authoritative location for a specific piece of information so it is not duplicated and always up to date
Using a single tool (e.g., Confluence) for all documentation
Requiring a single author to write all documentation
questions.explanation: SSOT means each fact, process, or decision has exactly one canonical source. Duplicating documentation causes drift - one version gets updated and the other doesn't, leading to conflicting information.

questions.q: What is 'information architecture' in the context of an internal wiki?
options: The technical architecture of the wiki platform (e.g., Confluence's data model)
The organization and hierarchy of wiki pages - how content is grouped, labeled, and navigated so users can find information efficiently
The process of backing up wiki content to a database
The decision about which wiki tool to use (Confluence vs. Notion vs. GitBook)
questions.explanation: Information architecture determines whether your wiki is findable. Poor IA means useful content exists but nobody can find it. Good IA uses clear naming, consistent structure, and logical groupings.

questions.q: What does 'orphaned page' mean in a wiki context?
options: A page that has not been edited in more than 6 months
A page that has no incoming links and is not part of any navigation tree, making it effectively invisible to most users
A page created by a former employee whose account was deleted
A page that was accidentally deleted and needs to be restored
questions.explanation: Orphaned pages exist in the wiki but are not linked from anywhere. They are invisible to users browsing the wiki unless they search specifically. Regular wiki audits should identify and link or archive orphaned pages.

questions.q: Which principle should guide the 'freshness' of a knowledge base article?
options: Articles should never be updated to preserve the historical record
Every article should display its last-reviewed date; articles not reviewed within a defined period should be flagged for review or marked as potentially outdated
Only senior engineers should be allowed to mark articles as current
Articles are considered fresh for one year, then automatically archived
questions.explanation: Knowledge bases degrade if not maintained. Displaying last-reviewed dates and flagging stale content (e.g., 'This article was last reviewed 8 months ago - verify before following') maintains reader trust.

questions.q: What is 'progressive disclosure' in knowledge base writing?
options: Gradually revealing company secrets to employees based on seniority
Structuring content so the most important information is presented first, with details available but not forced on readers who do not need them
Publishing documentation in stages as features are released
Requiring users to pass a quiz before accessing advanced documentation
questions.explanation: Progressive disclosure shows summaries first and lets readers drill down for details. A wiki article might start with a one-paragraph summary, then provide a detailed guide in expandable sections.

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'tagging' or 'labels' in a wiki or knowledge base?
options: To track which team member created each page
To categorize content so users can filter and find related articles across different sections of the wiki
To control which employees can edit specific pages
To mark pages that need to be translated into other languages
questions.explanation: Tags allow cross-cutting categorization. A page about 'deploying to production' might be tagged with both 'deployment' and 'on-call-runbook', making it findable via either tag even if its location in the wiki hierarchy is under 'operations'.

questions.q: Which sentence is an example of good knowledge base article writing?
options: This is the page about our deploy process. See the other pages for more info.

To deploy a hotfix to production: (1) create a branch from main, (2) push your fix, (3) open a PR tagged 'hotfix', (4) get approval from on-call lead, (5) merge - deployment runs automatically within 5 minutes.
Deployment can be complicated. Ask your team lead for help.
See Confluence for deployment documentation.
questions.explanation: Good knowledge base articles are actionable: numbered steps, specific commands or actions, expected outcomes. Vague references to other pages or team leads create friction and defeat the purpose of a knowledge base.

questions.q: John : "Hey team, I'm stuck on how to handle the new OAuth2 flow for our API. The documentation is…sparse."
options: Insufficient - John should just try debugging the code.
Correct - John needs a clear, documented guide to the OAuth2 flow with examples and troubleshooting tips.
Incorrect - John can figure it out himself by reading the existing API documentation thoroughly.
Incorrect - John should immediately ask a senior developer for help without explaining his issue.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights the need for an internal wiki or knowledge base. John's frustration demonstrates that the existing documentation is inadequate ; a well-maintained resource would provide step-by-step instructions, code examples (like the OAuth2 flow), and potential troubleshooting steps specifically tailored to the team's needs. Simply asking for help without context doesn't address the underlying issue of missing information-the goal is to proactively provide developers with the knowledge they need to solve problems quickly.

questions.q: Sarah : "Hey team, I'm reviewing this PR for the new user onboarding flow. The wiki article on 'Account Verification' is really unclear about the expected API response format after a successful verification attempt. It just says '200 OK' and doesn't provide any example JSON or details on what fields are required. This is making it difficult to validate the code against the specification."
options: Insufficient - the PR should automatically fix all documentation issues.
Correct - the documentation needs more detail, specifically a concrete API response example.
The PR is incorrect because it doesn't handle 200 OK responses.
Sarah's comment highlights a problem with the code implementation, not the documentation.
questions.explanation: This scenario focuses on a common pain point when developing internal knowledge bases. Sarah isn't simply stating that the documentation is bad; she's articulating a specific issue: a lack of concrete examples for the expected API response after account verification. The correct answer recognizes this needs to be addressed by adding more detail, particularly an example JSON payload, which would allow developers to accurately validate their code against the specification. The other options misinterpret Sarah's concern - it's about documentation clarity, not a direct bug in the PR itself.

questions.q: David : "I'm trying to troubleshoot this intermittent error with the payment processing service. I've added a comment to the relevant wiki page about it, but it still seems to be happening. Should I flag this for someone more senior?"
options: Immediately escalate to the DevOps team - they must have identified the root cause.
Ignore it; documenting issues is enough to track progress.
Document the steps you've taken and the symptoms, then monitor the page for updates or new comments. It's likely a transient issue or requires further investigation by someone with deeper access.
Delete the comment - it's cluttering the wiki and isn't contributing to a solution.
questions.explanation: The key here is understanding the role of a knowledge base in troubleshooting . Simply adding a comment doesn't guarantee resolution; rather, it should be part of a process of documenting and tracking an issue. Monitoring the page for updates or new comments demonstrates proactive engagement and allows others to contribute to the solution, while escalating immediately might be premature without further investigation. Deleting the comment would hinder collaborative problem-solving.

questions.q: John is writing a comment on the company wiki regarding a complex new feature. He writes: 'This page needs more detail about how to handle rate limiting with the external service. It just mentions 'respect the limits' - that's not helpful!' Which of the following best describes John 's concern and what action he should take regarding this wiki page?
options: Insufficient - the page simply needs a more detailed explanation of rate limiting.
Critical - the lack of specific guidance could lead to service degradation and potential outages, requiring immediate attention.
Minor - it's just a suggestion for improvement; John should politely request an update from the author.
Neutral - rate limiting is a common concern and this page addresses it adequately without further detail.
questions.explanation: John 's comment highlights a significant issue: vague guidance can have serious consequences in a technical environment. Simply stating 'respect the limits' isn't actionable; developers need concrete details about thresholds, error handling, and potential impact. The correct answer reflects this urgency - rate limiting failures can directly affect service availability and performance, making immediate attention crucial for mitigation and preventing further problems. Options A & B are too simplistic; Option C minimizes the problem's severity, while Option D is completely inaccurate.

questions.q: Sarah is reviewing a PR and notices the wiki article on 'Account Verification' lacks crucial details. The article simply states '200 OK' after successful verification but doesn't provide example JSON or required field information. This makes validating the code difficult. Which of the following actions best addresses Sarah 's concern regarding the wiki page?
options: Immediately edit the wiki article to include a detailed example JSON response, citing the API specification as the definitive source.
Flag the PR for review by the API team, requesting they update the specification before the code can be validated.
Add a comment to the wiki page referencing the specification and suggesting that the developers add an example JSON response to the article based on the spec. This would provide immediate clarity .
Ignore the issue - the PR is already approved, and the developers should figure out how to handle the response format themselves.
questions.explanation: The correct answer highlights the importance of providing concrete examples within a knowledge base. Simply stating '200 OK' is insufficient; developers need tangible data to understand expected behavior and validate their code. Flagging for the API team (Option B) delays progress unnecessarily. Editing immediately (Option A) without referencing the source specification could introduce inaccuracies, while ignoring the problem (Option D) is a poor solution as it leaves the developer struggling. Providing an example based on the specification ensures consistency and clarity within the knowledge base .
